prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "BHP Group Ltd" (ticker BHP), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BHP", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: BHP Group Limited
result.industry: Diversified mining (copper, iron ore, steelmaking coal, potash)
markets: By-products: gold, silver, uranium, molybdenum, zinc

mission.statement: To bring people and resources together to build a better world.
mission.plain: BHP wants to dig up the raw materials the world needs and do it in a way that leaves things better.

about.plain: BHP is one of the biggest mining companies in the world. It digs copper out of huge mines in Chile and South Australia and iron ore out of the ground in Western Australia. It ships these rocks and metals to factories, mostly in Asia, that turn them into wires, steel and other materials. It is also building a giant new mine in Canada for potash, a mineral farmers use to help crops grow.
about.customers: Steel mills, copper smelters and metal traders, mostly in China and the rest of Asia.
about.everyday: The copper in your phone charger cable and house wiring, and the steel in cars and buildings, may well have started as rock dug up by BHP.

money.plain: copper plus gold, silver, uranium and molybdenum from Chile and South Australia
iron ore from the Pilbara in Western Australia, used to make steel
steelmaking coal from Queensland and power-station coal from New South Wales
leftover nickel sales; the nickel business was put into temporary suspension in December 2024
crop fertiliser from a new Canadian mine; Stage 1 first production expected mid-2027

result.summary: BHP has a real but commodity-style advantage: it owns some of the world's largest, lowest-cost, long-life deposits, notably Escondida (the world's largest copper mine) and the Pilbara iron ore system, which its FY2026 results call the lowest-cost major iron ore operation globally. That cost position earned a 59% Underlying EBITDA margin and 26.1% underlying return on capital in FY2026, but BHP cannot set prices, so its edge is surviving and earning through the cycle rather than pricing power.

pricingPower.evidence: BHP is a price-taker on index-linked commodities: revenue fell from $65,098M in FY2022 to $51,262M in FY2025 as iron ore prices fell, then rose to $58,760M in FY2026 mainly on copper prices; in 2025-26 China's state buyer CMRG banned purchases of several BHP iron ore products for more than six months (lifted 14 April 2026), showing that a concentrated buyer can push back on terms.

moats.evidence: Iron ore and copper are sold on specification and index prices, so the BHP name earns no price premium with end consumers; its reputation helps mainly with governments, partners and lenders.
Steel mills tune their blends to particular ore products such as Newman fines, but they can and did swap to other suppliers' cargoes when CMRG restricted BHP products in 2025-26.
A tonne of ore is no more valuable to one buyer because other buyers also use BHP; there is no network effect.

WAIO's FY2026 C1 cash cost was $16.40/t with a target below $19/t on the reported unit-cost measure, and Escondida's unit cost was $1.07/lb; these sit at the bottom of their cost curves and gave Copper a 70% and Iron Ore a 61% Underlying EBITDA margin in FY2026.

Integrated Pilbara mine-rail-port networks need tens of billions of dollars and decades to build, so seaborne iron ore is effectively an oligopoly of Rio Tinto, Vale, BHP and Fortescue; new entrants such as Simandou take many years.
BHP competes with the same business model as other majors; there is no incumbent unable to copy it.

Decades of operating very large mines, autonomous haulage and integrated logistics underpin record WAIO production and the 10% fall in Escondida unit costs in FY2026, but rivals have similar capabilities.

BHP controls tier-one, multi-decade orebodies such as Escondida, Olympic Dam in Copper South Australia, the Pilbara tenements and the Jansen potash deposit, which BHP expects to run for more than 60 years; deposits like these cannot be recreated.

customers.evidence: Customers are a small number of large Asian steel mills and smelters with long relationships, and the incoming CEO met China Baowu's chairman to help end the CMRG ban; the 2025-26 restrictions on Jimblebar, Jinbao and Newman fines show that loyalty is commercial and depends on price, not attachment.

talent.evidence: BHP is a sought-after employer in Australian and Chilean mining, and its CEO says it is the only global listed miner to have reached gender balance across its workforce; it still competes for scarce mining engineers, and a contractor was fatally injured at BMA in 2026.

product.evidence: Its products are standard commodities; quality and cost come from the orebody (BMA is one of the largest suppliers of higher-quality steelmaking coal), but Pilbara fines are mid-grade compared with Vale's higher-grade Brazilian ore.

competitors.name: Rio Tinto
competitors.note: Pilbara iron ore (326.2 Mt shipped in 2025), copper (Oyu Tolgoi, Kennecott) and aluminium; BHP's closest diversified peer.

competitors.name: Vale
competitors.note: Brazil's iron ore giant and BHP's main rival in seaborne iron ore; also nickel and copper.

competitors.name: Fortescue
competitors.note: Pure-play Pilbara iron ore producer selling to Chinese mills.

competitors.name: Freeport-McMoRan
competitors.note: Large listed copper producer (Grasberg, Americas); competes for copper concentrate and cathode buyers.

competitors.name: Codelco
competitors.note: Chilean state copper producer operating next to BHP's Escondida and Pampa Norte.

competitors.name: Anglo American (merging with Teck to form Anglo Teck)
competitors.note: Copper in Chile and Peru, Kumba iron ore and premium steelmaking coal; BHP made and dropped takeover approaches in 2024 and November 2025.

competitors.name: Glencore
competitors.note: Copper, Australian thermal and steelmaking coal, and commodity trading.

competitors.name: Southern Copper
competitors.note: Low-cost copper mines in Peru and Mexico.

competitors.name: Teck Resources
competitors.note: Copper (Quebrada Blanca, Antamina stake) and zinc; merging with Anglo American.

competitors.name: Zijin Mining
competitors.note: Fast-growing Chinese copper and gold miner.

competitors.name: Nutrien
competitors.note: World's largest potash producer, also in Saskatchewan; the main future rival to Jansen.

competitors.name: Mosaic
competitors.note: Potash and phosphate producer with Saskatchewan potash mines.

competitors.name: Simandou partners (Rio Tinto, Winning Consortium, Chinalco)
competitors.note: New high-grade Guinea iron ore supply that could add to seaborne competition.

competitors.name: Coronado Global Resources
competitors.note: Queensland and US steelmaking coal producer competing with BMA.

marketShare.measure: tonnes of copper mined (company production / USGS 2025 world mine production of 23,000 thousand t; BHP uses its fiscal year to June 2026)
tonnes (BHP WAIO FY2026 production 291.2 Mt and Rio Tinto 2025 Pilbara shipments 326.2 Mt, both 100% basis / USGS 2025e world usable ore 2,600 Mt)

threats: Chinese steel demand slowdown and a property downturn weighing on iron ore prices, which fell into the low-$100s/t in 2026
Concentrated Chinese buying power through China Mineral Resources Group (CMRG), which banned several BHP iron ore products from September 2025 until April 2026
New high-grade supply from Simandou in Guinea adding to the seaborne iron ore market
Falling copper grades and output: FY2027 copper guidance of 1,650-1,800 kt versus 1,953 kt in FY2026, with Escondida unit costs guided up to $1.20-1.50/lb
Jansen potash cost overruns: Stage 2 estimate raised from $4.9bn to $6.9bn and a $2.3bn Jansen-related impairment in FY2026
Resource nationalism, higher royalties and water or permitting limits in Chile, Australia and Canada
Legacy liabilities such as the Samarco dam failure in Brazil and safety incidents (a contractor fatality at BMA in 2026)

ceo.name: Brandon Craig
ceo.background: Mechanical engineer (BEng) with a master's in business leadership from the University of Natal; more than 25 years at BHP, including head of Western Australia Iron Ore and President Americas from 2024

c1.evidence: BHP calls itself the world's largest copper producer (about 2 Mt in FY2026), and copper is a growing market tied to electrification, but mining is a mature industry, not an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Customers buy BHP ore for reliable volume and specification at index prices, not for brand; its lasting edge is low-cost tier-one deposits like Escondida and the Pilbara, which are hard to copy.

c3.evidence: BHP is a household name in Australia and the default 'Big Australian' miner, but most consumers elsewhere don't know it and never buy its products directly.

c4.evidence: Its purpose is 'to bring people and resources together to build a better world', and it stresses decarbonisation and future-facing commodities, but management is judged mainly on returns and dividends (72% payout in FY2026).

c6.evidence: “big Australian miner, iron ore, dividends, Samarco” — the impression is mostly of a solid, profitable mining giant, mixed with environmental and safety concerns.

c7.evidence: Copper and potash demand rides electrification, grid build-out and food security, and BHP says its pipeline could lift copper output about 40% by FY35, but iron ore and coal (about half of FY2026 revenue) face flat or declining Chinese steel demand.

c8.evidence: BHP is expanding into potash (Jansen Stage 1 first production mid-2027, Stage 2 late FY31) and copper growth in Chile, Argentina (Vicuña) and Arizona (Resolution), but it stays a mining company.

m1.evidence: Brandon Craig, CEO since 1 July 2026, has set out a copper-led growth plan ('copper is the engine that is driving BHP's growth'), a clear but conventional strategy.

m2.evidence: Craig is a career BHP executive with more than 25 years at the company, not a founder; BHP was founded in 1885.

m4.evidence: Craig talks about safety and customer relationships, especially in China, but there is little independent evidence on his servant-leadership style yet.

m5.evidence: BHP has a strong operating culture focused on safety and productivity, and it reports gender balance across its workforce, but it is not known for inventing new products.

m6.evidence: Craig is a mechanical engineer who started in maintenance and engineering roles and ran Western Australia Iron Ore operations, delivering the South Flank mine.

m7.evidence: Craig has been CEO only since July 2026; there is no strong public record either way beyond BHP's stated focus on safety, Indigenous partnerships and lower emissions.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Brandon Craig at a top university could be found.

m8b.evidence: Craig is a low-profile operational leader, not a celebrity CEO.

m9.evidence: At WAIO he delivered South Flank and helped make it the lowest-cost major iron ore producer, and as President Americas from 2024 he oversaw Escondida's improved grade and production guidance.

m10.evidence: BHP is cost-focused, targeting WAIO unit costs below $19/t, but it is not known for a frugality culture like Amazon's.

c10.evidence: Its copper, iron ore and coal end up in power grids, buildings and vehicles used by billions of people, but indirectly and as a replaceable supplier.

p2.evidence: Building and running mines like Escondida or the $8.4bn Jansen Stage 1 takes decades and billions of dollars, and the metals are vital to electrification and steel.

f1.evidence: Revenue went $56,921M (FY2021), $65,098M, $53,817M, $55,658M, $51,262M and $58,760M (FY2026), falling in two of the last five years.

f2.evidence: Profit from operations as a share of revenue fell from 44.8% in FY2021 and 52.4% in FY2022 to 40.6% in FY2026; BHP does not report a gross margin.

f3.evidence: Net debt was $8.7bn at 30 June 2026, about 0.3x Underlying EBITDA of $32.9bn, against $18,532M of cash and total equity of $56,321M.

f4.evidence: Profit from operations fell from $25,515M in FY2021 to $23,869M in FY2026 (after a peak of $34,106M in FY2022); operating cash flow was $21,778M in FY2026 versus $20,665M in FY2024.

v1.evidence: BHP's copper and iron ore are not different from rivals' in a way an ordinary buyer would notice; its advantage is lower cost, with the lowest-cost major iron ore operation and a 70% copper EBITDA margin in FY2026.

v2.evidence: BHP is a well-regarded Australian employer and reports gender balance across its workforce, but no verified current top-company ranking was found.

c5.evidence: If BHP disappeared, Chinese steel mills, copper smelters and the Australian and Chilean economies would notice right away, but other miners would fill the gap over time at higher prices.
